Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa
------------------------------------------
Out of the six subsidiary works known as ‘Vedāṅgas’ (‘limbs of the वेदस्’) the कल्पसूत्रस् deal mainly with sacri-ficial rites. (See KALPASŪTRAS.) To fill up the gaps as it were and to expound details not mentioned in these works, but needed for the meticulous performance of the sacrificial rites, some compendiums were composed and they were called ‘pariśiṣṭas’ (‘what is left over,’ appendix). गोभिल-saṅgraha-परिशिष्ट is one such work related to the सामवेद. Based on this work, कात्यायन (4th to 6th cent. A.D.) wrote a work called Karmapradīpa. This work is known by several other names such as ‘Sāmagṛhya,’ ‘Chāndogyapariśiṣṭa,’ ‘Chandogapariśiṣṭa’ and also, ‘Gobhila-स्मृति.’ It contains about 500 verses.
This work deals with the topics of wearing the sacred thread, worship of गणेश and other deities, śrāddha (obsequial rites), consecration of sacred fires, सन्ध्या ritual, the five daily sacrifices, rules of personal cleanliness and cere-monial purity, duties of a wife and so on.

Chandas
(‘that which exhilarates’)
------------------------------------------
One of the names by which the वेदस् are called, is ‘chandas,’ ‘that which exhilarates’ or ‘that which gives a (protective) covering’. More commonly, however, it denotes the metres in poetry. Vedic prosody called ‘Chandas,’ or ‘Chandaś-śāstra,’ is considered as one of the six ‘Vedāṅgas’ or ‘limbs of the Veda’ (subsidiary disciplines pertaining to the field of Vedic studies), without a study of which, it will be impossible to understand the वेदस् proper. Before reciting the Vedic mantras (chants or hymns) it is obligatory to pay one’s respect to the ṛṣi (sage through whom the मन्त्र was revealed), the devatā (the deity to whom it is addressed) and the छन्दस् (the metre in which the मन्त्र is composed).
The earliest of the extant works on Vedic prosody is the छन्दस्-sūtra by Piṅgala (2nd cent. B.C.) which is in the form of sūtras or aphorisms spread over eight chapters. Eleven major and many more minor metres have been dealt with in this work. गायत्री, uṣṇik, anuṣṭup, triṣṭup, जगती, बृहती and paṅkti are the more common ones among them. Usually each metre consists of one to five pādas or ‘feet’ and each pāda should consist of a specific number of letters. For instance, the famous गायत्री metre consists of three pādas and eight letters per pāda. The various metres found in classical Sanskrit literature were gradually evolved from the Vedic metres.
It was believed that the use of certain metres was conducive to the attainment of power or could bring about harm to the enemies.

Chāndogya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Among the six traditional systems of Hindu philosophy known as षड्-दर्शनस्, the Vedānta system, undoubtedly, gets the pride of place. This system, which is very much alive even in the modern times and quite popular, is based entirely on the उपनिषद्स्, the predominantly philosophical sections of the वेदस्. The छान्दोग्य उपनिषद् is one of the ten उपनिषद्स् considered to be ancient and authoritative, and on which शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) has written a voluminous commentary. Its importance can be judged from the fact that the work ब्रह्मसूत्रस् has drawn heavily upon it, for topics of discussion.
Though the word ‘chandas’ (‘that which exhilarates’) is one of the names of the वेदस् in general, it is more particularly applied to the सामवेद, the third of the four वेदस् wherein the mantras, known as ‘sāmans,’ are set to मुसिच् and sung. Those who have specialized in the singing of these sāmans, are called ‘Chandogas’ and the ब्राह्मण (liturgical section) pertaining to them is designated as Chāndogya ब्राह्मण, which itself forms a part of the Tāṇḍya branch of the सामवेद. This ब्राह्मण contains ten prapāṭhakas or sections out of which the first two form the मन्त्र ब्राह्मण and the rest, छान्दोग्य उपनिषद्. It comprises eight chapters and each is subdivided into ‘khaṇḍas’ or sections (total number of khaṇḍas being 154) and contains 628 kaṇḍikās or mantras, all in prose.
First Chapter
The speciality of this Upaniṣad is that it describes a number of ‘upāsanās’ or ‘vidyās’ or meditations, based generally on Vedic rituals. Since the average spiritual aspirant has devoted the major part of his life to the performance of these rituals, it will be rather difficult for him to take to meditation on God straight away. Hence he is led to it gradually by a series of graded meditations on the rituals, each of the parts being substituted by appropriate symbols that elevate the whole process to spiritual levels. The entire first chapter is devoted to one such meditation, that on the ‘udgītha,’ the principal part of a सामन् chant. Since the उद्गीथ invariably starts with Oṁ and Oṁ is the best symbol of परमात्मन्, the Supreme Self or God, the Upaniṣad begins with its upāsanā. The second section, with the help of an ancient anecdote, stresses the importance of meditation on the उद्गीथ as identified with the mukhyaprāṇa, the primary life force within the body, which at the cosmic level, has manifested itself as the sun. meditation on Oṁ in various aspects is continued till the 7th section. The twelfth section gives an amusing incident of dogs singing उद्गीथ (hence called ‘śauva-उद्गीथ,’ śauva = related to dogs) for obtaining ड़ोओद्. शङ्कर opines that some supernatural deities assuming the forms of dogs revealed this उद्गीथ to the sage बक-दाल्भ्य, and it helps a hungry person in securing ड़ोओद्.
Second Chapter
If the first chapter concentrated on prescribing meditation on the different parts or limbs of the सामन्, the second chapter is devoted to meditations on the whole सामन्. Sections 2 to 10 deal mainly with such meditations. Sections 11 to 21 deal with the meditations on certain special sāmans like the gāyatrasāman, rathantara-सामन्, revatīsāman and so on. The twenty-third section, which mentions about the four āśramas or stages of life, deals with the result of meditating purely on Oṁ, which is the attainment of इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
Third Chapter
The first eleven sections of the third chapter deal with the meditation on the आदित्य or the sun, who is the personification of the results of all sacrifices, as also the karmas of all beings. The whole series of meditations are called मधु-विद्या, since आदित्य has been compared to ‘madhu’ or honey. Sections 12 and 13 deal with meditation on ब्रह्मन् through the गायत्री since that is the best among the Vedic metres. meditation on ब्रह्मन् in the space or ether of the heart, which is identical with the space or ether outside has also been described. The 14th section gives the famous शाण्डिल्यविद्या. It prescribes meditation on the आत्मन् in the lotus of one’s heart, but as identified with ब्रह्मन्, called here as ‘tajjalān.’ This leads to the attainment of ब्रह्मन्, after the fall of the body. Sections 15 and 16 deal with Kośavidyā for the longevity of one’s son and पुरुषविद्या for one’s own longevity. The sage Mahidāsa ऐतरेय who discovered the latter विद्या is said to have lived for 116 years.
Fourth Chapter
The fourth chapter describes four important विद्यास्: सṁवर्गविद्या, Ṣoḍaśa-kalavidyā, उपकोसलविद्या and Akṣi-पुरुषविद्या. जानश्रुति Pautrāyaṇa, a king well-known for his generosity, comes to know of the spiritual eminence of the sage रैक्व through the accidental hearing of a conversation between two swans flying over his palace. After a thorough search he discovers रैक्व resting in the shade under a cart. Honouring him suitably with presents, the king seeks spiritual wisdom from him. रैक्व teaches him to meditate upon वायु (cosmic wind) outside and the mukhya-प्राण (chief life-force) inside, as ‘saṁvarga,’ i.e., one which absorbs and dissolves everything within itself. ‘Saṁvarga’ is प्रजापति, the Self of all gods. This is the subject-matter of the first three sections. The touching story of the young boy Satyakāma Jābāla and the Ṣoḍaśakalavidyā he received directly from supernatural deities has been described in sections 4 to 9. meditation on ब्रह्मन्, the final cause of this world, through meditation on its 16 ‘kalas’ or parts or aspects, is the subject matter of this particular विद्या. Sections 10 to 14 deal with the story of उपकोसल, a disciple of Satyakāma and his obtaining knowledge of ब्रह्मन् from the three sacred fires in the होउसे of his गुरु. This has been called उपकोसलविद्या. The fires taught that प्राण or the chief life-force, manifesting in the heart as bliss, is ब्रह्मन्. The teacher Satyakāma completed their teaching by imparting the knowledge of the ‘akṣipuruṣa,’ the power behind the senses, the आत्मन्. One who realizes this आत्मन् goes to the abode of ब्रह्मन् after death and does not return to transmi-gratory existence.
Fifth Chapter
The fifth chapter puts before us three kinds of destination for a सोउल् after the death of the body:
Those practising पञ्चाग्निविद्या (‘meditation on the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’) and similar other upāsanās will go by the ‘arcirādi-mārga’ or the path of light, to ब्रह्मलोक, the abode of ब्रह्मन् and will not return to transmigratory worlds.
Those who perform only rituals without enlightenment will travel by the ‘dhūmādi-mārga,’ the path of smoke, and attain the worlds like पितृलोक or the world of manes, from which they return to the human world after some time.
Those who lead a beastly life without practising either upāsanās or ritualistic karmas, will constantly go through the rounds of birth and death.
The first two sections prescribe meditation on the mukhya-प्राण, the chief life-force, after establishing its superiority over other prāṇas (the sense-organs) through an anecdote. Sections 3 to 10 deal with the famous पञ्चाग्निविद्या (‘the doctrine of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’) and एस्छतोलोग्य्. Young श्वेतकेतु, puffed up with the pride of learning, goes to the court of the king प्रवाहण जैवलि, with a view to establishing the superiority of his learning but is rebuffed by the king who knew better. He returns crestfallen and angry to his ड़थेर्, the sage गौतम. गौतम approaches the king प्रवाहण जैवलि in all humility and requests him to teach the पञ्चाग्निविद्या about which he had questioned श्वेतकेतु earlier. In this विद्या, heavenly world, rains, earth, man and woman are to be contemplated upon as fire into which oblations of faith, subtle body (of the sacrificer), rain, ड़ोओद् and semen are poured, the final oblation being responsible for the rebirth of the sacrificer. Those who know this science go to the world of ब्रह्मन् after death and will not return here. The rest of the chapter (sections 11 to 24) deals with the Vaiśvānaravidyā. Six sages under the leadership of उद्दालक आरुणि obtain this विद्या from the king अश्वपति Kaikeya who was an adept in it. वैश्वानर आत्मन् is ईश्वर or the Cosmic Being, pervading the universe. He is also inside us as the chief life-force, mukhya-प्राण. Hence the act of eating ड़ोओद् should be contemplated upon as अग्निहोत्र sacrifice. One who achieves perfection in this will become identified with the Cosmic Being. This is the gist of this विद्या.
Sixth Chapter
The last three chapters—6th, 7th and 8th—contain the quintessence of the Vedānta philosophy. The whole of the sixth chapter is devoted to a delineation of the Sadvidyā, knowledge and meditation pertaining to Sat (the eternal Truth) or ब्रह्मन्. It is in the form of a dialogue between the son श्वेतकेतु and his ड़थेर् उद्दालक आरुणि. When श्वेतकेतु returns home after completing a twelve-year course in Vedic studies, the ड़थेर् उद्दालक आरुणि notices his conceit born of that learning and questions him whether he has known that by knowing which everything will be known. However, the boy had not known it and so requests his ड़थेर् himself to teach it to him. Citing the examples of clay, gold and iron, and their products (like pot, ornament and nail-cutter) the ड़थेर् first draws the attention of his son to the identity between the cause and its effects, pointing out that names and forms are unreal, the substance alone being real. Applying this principle, he states that before च्रेअतिओन्, Sat (the eternal Truth) alone existed and that Sat evolved into this world of names and forms through the three primary elements: तेजस् (fire), ap (water) and अन्न (earth). All objects of च्रेअतिओन् including the bodies of living beings, have come out of these elements through permutation and combination. This is the gist of the teachings of the first seven sections. Sections 8 to 10 deal with the merging of the individual self, the जीव, into Sat during the state of deep sleep. However, since इग्नोरन्चे persists, he comes back to his original state. The same लोगिच् applies in the case of rebirth after death also. But, those who attain knowledge will get liberated. The famous Vedāntic dictum tat tvam asi, ‘That thou art’, appears for the first time in the eighth section and is repeated later, nine times. Sections 12 and 13 teach that Sat, the primary Cause of the universe, is too subtle to be perceived even as the seed of the banyan tree in which the whole tree exists in an involved state. But it pervades the entire च्रेअतिओन् like the lump of salt dissolved in a jar of water. To know this Sat, the help of a teacher, गुरु or guide, is necessary. It is like a blindfolded traveller, let off in a forest by robbers, finding his way out with the help of a kind सोउल्. This is the teaching of the 14th section. Though the mode of death is similar to the ignorant as well as the enlightened souls, the latter will not transmigrate whereas the former do. This is explained in the last two sections with the help of an anecdote of the police catching a thief. The purport of the whole chapter seems to be to teach the identity of the jīvātman or the individual self with ब्रह्मन्, the Cosmic सोउल्.
Seventh Chapter
The seventh chapter teaches Bhūma-विद्या, knowledge of the Infinite. नारद, though himself a great sage and a man of considerable erudition, approaches the distinguished sage Sanatkumāra with a heavy heart seeking peace and joy. Sanatkumāra takes him step by step through meditations on fifteen objects like name, speech, मिन्द् and so on, to भूमन्, the Infinite. The भूमन् which is everywhere, which is established in its own glory, by knowing which there is nothing else to be known, is the Self of all beings. One who realizes it, becomes ‘svarāṭ.’ Like a king, he will have full freedom in all the worlds. To obtain this knowledge, purity of मिन्द् got through purity of ड़ोओद् and purity of sense-experience, is necessary. It is only a pure मिन्द् that can retain and realize spiritual truths.
Eighth Chapter
It is rather difficult to comprehend and contemplate upon ब्रह्मन् without qualities, described as Sat and भूमन्. It is easier to meditate upon the saguṇa or qualified aspect of ब्रह्मन्, as possessing of blessed qualities. The eighth chapter prescribes such a meditation on ब्रह्मन् in the region of one’s heart, as also related disciplines like ब्रह्मचर्य. The first two sections deal with Dahara-विद्या, meditation on ब्रह्मन् in the ‘daharākāśa,’ the little space in the region of the heart. This आकाश or space in the heart is itself ब्रह्मन्. It is not limited to that spatial area nor does it get destroyed with the destruction of the body. One who realizes this obtains whatever he wants, in whichever world he contemplates. The next three sections extol and prescribe ब्रह्मचर्य or celibacy and other related disciplines, for realizing the आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन्, who like a dyke is protecting all the worlds. The sixth section describes the various nāḍīs or passages for the flow of prāṇic energy and how the सोउल् of a man of knowledge, at the time of death, enters into सुषुम्ना nāḍī, departs through the aperture in the top of the head and reaches ब्रह्मलोक, the abode of ब्रह्मन्, from which there is no return. Sections 7 to 12 deal with the teachings of प्रजापति to इन्द्र and विरोचन. Hearing from प्रजापति, the ड़थेर् of च्रेअतिओन्, that one who realizes the आत्मन्, the Self, who is sinless and beyond all limitations like hunger and thirst, old-age and death, इन्द्र the king of gods and विरोचन the king of demons decided to get that knowledge of the आत्मन्. After undergoing ब्रह्मचर्य (disciplines necessary for spiritual studies) for 32 years, they both approached him for the teaching. When प्रजापति said, that the ‘person seen in the eye’ is the आत्मन्, विरोचन understood it as the reflection seen in the eyeball, which again is the body. Fully satisfied with this understanding that the body is itself the आत्मन्, he returned to his tribe and taught it to them. इन्द्र too took it that way; but very soon he got doubts since the body which is seen in the reflection, is subject to mutilation, disease and death, whereas the आत्मन् is not. He returned and expressed his doubts when प्रजापति instructed him, after a further period of ब्रह्मचर्य for 32 years, that the ‘person who moves about in the dream is the आत्मन्.’ When इन्द्र discovered the limitations of this teaching as also of the next that ‘the person in dreamless sleep is the आत्मन्,’ he was truly instructed (after further periods of ब्रह्मचर्य totalling in all, 101 years) that the आत्मन् is the ‘seer’ behind the eyes and all other sense organs, is the witness of all the states and is the immortal spirit different from the mortal body. The last section gives the list of teachers of spiritual wisdom. It also adds that one who leads a life in accordance with धर्म and meditates on ब्रह्मन् in the heart, will reach Brahma-लोक after death and will not return.
Epilogue
Apart from the fact that this Upaniṣad is the second longest and one of the more ancient ones, it throws an interesting light on contemporary history and customs. It mentions many geographical names like Pāñcāla, कुरु, Naimiṣa, गान्धार and Kekaya. References to many sciences and arts, villages and towns, buildings and parts of buildings, tools of iron and other implements, different kinds of articles of ड़ोओद् and drink, musical instruments, minerals and metals mentioned by name, carts and chariots, keepers of cows and horses, kings and law-enforcing agencies, several calendaric terms—all these indicate a fair degree of civilization. Family life was highly valued and social life was generally peaceful. Truth and righteousness were given the pride of place. For acquiring knowledge from competent teachers no sacrifice was considered too great. The teachers also enforced discipline strictly. Though ritua-listic religion was very much in vogue, philosophical inquiry was considered a superior pursuit.
Thus, the छान्दोग्य उपनिषद् is a unique text of the Vedānta system giving an insight into a philosophical inquiry of the highest kind.
See also UPANIṢADS and VIDYĀS.
